content.title: Being a change agent
content.subtitle: One of 61 to make history
content.summary: Masoomi succeeded in securing admission to the diploma programme in Faizabad, run by the Badakhshan Provincial Public Health Directorate & the Badakhshan Institute of Health Sciences, with technical support from the AKU's Programmes in Afghanistan.

content.text: For Zainub Masoomi the challenges of being a nurse became evident as a final-year student of the General Nursing Diploma programme, when she was asked to make home visits as part of the community-based practice component of the course.

"People simply refused to talk to us when we visited them," recalls Masoomi. "Some of them refused to open their doors even during the winter with rain or snow falling on our faces. We requested our management and faculty to let us pull back from community practice. However, they were adamant: each one of us needed to understand the importance of working with families in the communities, each one of us would be agents of change. So we went back to our work in the communities, we tried to resolve issues and at the end were able to change quite a lot of preconceived notions."

Masoomi persevered because she realised that so much depended on her success. Health care services in her home district, Wardooj, are extremely limited and maternal and child mortality rates high. There are very few nurses and nursing is a relatively unknown profession.

Three years ago, Masoomi succeeded in securing admission to the diploma programme in Faizabad, run by the Badakhshan Provincial Public Health Directorate and the Badakhshan Institute of Health Sciences, with technical support from the Aga Khan University's Programmes in Afghanistan.
Although excited to be admitted into the nursing profession she was worried about whether she could cope with the tough studies ahead.

But the programme provided an environment that helped students attain a high level of learning. The faculty constantly used methods and strategies to actively involve students in the learning, based on their level of understanding and comprehension. The friendly atmosphere added to her interest in nursing.

Initially, it was hard to adjust to the new environment at the women's hostel. "Each one of us came from diverse backgrounds, spoke different dialects and practiced different faiths. But with increased awareness, knowledge, and critical thinking and problem-solving skills, I learned how to deal with difficult situations," recalls Masoomi.
Today, Masoomi is one among the 61 students who have made history in Afghanistan, earning the Best Graduate Award from a nursing course in Faizabad, Badakhshan.

"As a certified nurse, I wish to change negative attitudes about nursing. This can only be done by providing quality nursing services to the public. I will show my people the importance of nursing and how to lead healthy lifestyles. I firmly believe that nursing is a second name for serving people with honesty and commitment," says a determined Masoomi.
